question.stem:
A company has hundreds of VPCs with multiple VPN connections to their data centers spanning 5 AWS Regions. As the number of its workloads grows, the company must be able to scale its networks across multiple accounts and VPCs to keep up. A Solutions Architect is tasked to interconnect all of the company’s on-premises networks, VPNs, and VPCs into a single gateway, which includes support for inter-region peering across multiple AWS regions.
Which of the following is the BEST solution that the architect should set up to support the required interconnectivity?
options: Set up an AWS Direct Connect Gateway to achieve inter-region VPC access to all of the AWS resources and on-premises data centers. Set up a link aggregation group (LAG) to aggregate multiple connections at a single AWS Direct Connect endpoint in order to treat them as a single, managed connection. Launch a virtual private gateway in each VPC and then create a public virtual interface for each AWS Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect Gateway.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway in each region to interconnect all networks within it. Then, route traffic between the transit gateways through a peering connection.

Enable inter-region VPC peering that allows peering relationships to be established between multiple VPCs across different AWS regions. Set up a networking configuration that ensures that the traffic will always stay on the global AWS backbone and never traverse the public Internet.

Set up an AWS VPN CloudHub for inter-region VPC access and a Direct Connect gateway for the VPN connections to the on-premises data centers. Create a virtual private gateway in each VPC, then create a private virtual interface for each AWS Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect gateway.
question.explanation: AWS Transit Gateway is the hub that connects VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect (through a Direct Connect gateway) with transitive routing and scales to thousands of attachments. A Transit Gateway is Regional, so with 5 Regions you deploy one per Region and connect them with Transit Gateway peering attachments, which gives inter-Region connectivity over the AWS backbone. VPC peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link, so hundreds of VPCs would need a full mesh. A Direct Connect gateway (with VGWs and a public virtual interface, which is not even valid for this) and VPN CloudHub do not interconnect hundreds of VPCs across Regions.

concept: Transit Gateway per Region + TGW peering: interconnect hundreds of VPCs, VPNs and Regions
tests: Choosing Transit Gateways (one per Region, joined by TGW peering) to interconnect hundreds of VPCs, VPNs and on-premises networks across Regions, instead of VPC peering, Direct Connect gateway or VPN CloudHub.
expected: One Transit Gateway per Region, VPCs and VPNs attached to it, Transit Gateways peered across Regions (static routes), shared with RAM across accounts. Triggers: 'hundreds of VPCs', 'single gateway', 'multiple accounts', 'inter-Region peering', 'VPN connections'.
why_not: A Direct Connect gateway connects on-premises to VPCs through VGWs and does not give VPC-to-VPC transitive routing; a public virtual interface is also the wrong type for private VPC access. Inter-Region VPC peering is non-transitive and one-to-one, so hundreds of VPCs mean a huge full mesh, not a single gateway. VPN CloudHub links branch offices through one VGW in a hub-and-spoke VPN, it is not an inter-Region VPC fabric and is not combined with a Direct Connect gateway this way.
